app.title: Exceedance curves (Кривые обеспеченности)
app.summary: A person loads a spreadsheet of observations, picks the value column, can group rows by a column such as year and reduce each group to its maximum, minimum, mean or sum, and can drop single points from the series. They pick a curve mode: ordinary, truncated to a row range or value band, or compound, where the series is split into two parts that are fitted separately. They then fit one or more theoretical probability distributions to the empirical exceedance points, read goodness-of-fit metrics and design quantiles at standard exceedance probabilities, and can add their own probability or return period to the table. Finally they download a Word report with the series, the empirical table, the curve plot and the tables.

task.text: Fit probability distributions to a series of extremes and read off design values at chosen exceedance probabilities or return periods.

data.text: A spreadsheet of observations with a numeric value column and optional grouping columns. It is reduced to one value per group, such as an annual maximum, and ranked into an empirical exceedance series.
data.item: one value in the series, such as the maximum for one year

stage.text: frequency analysis of a prepared observation series, before writing up design values

mechanism.text: Four tabs run in order: load, prepare, process and results. Each tab waits until the one before it has produced something. In the process tab, the chosen curve mode and distributions redraw an exceedance-probability chart over the empirical points, and the colour-coded fit metrics and quantile tables update with it, with linked inputs for probability and return period.

field.text: flood frequency analysis of hydrometeorological series in hydrology

workflow.name: fit candidate distributions to a series and read off design quantiles

steps.here: Upload an Excel workbook or press the button that loads the bundled sample file. A collapsed preview shows the first rows.

steps.step: reduce the raw table to one series
steps.here: Pick the numeric values column and an optional grouping column with an aggregate (max, min, mean or sum). Rows with empty values are listed and dropped, and a line chart shows the resulting series.
A multiselect of 'group – value' labels removes single points before ranking. A truncated mode keeps only a row range or a value band.

steps.step: compute a value from the data
steps.here: Values are ranked into empirical exceedance probabilities m/(n+1). Selected distributions (Gumbel, Pearson III, GEV, Krytsky–Menkel; fitted by MLE, moments or L-moments) are fitted and drawn on a probability axis with a return-period scale.
A metrics table gives mean, Cv, Cs, R², MAE, maxE and Anderson–Darling for each distribution against the empirical series, coloured green to red by how good each fit is.
A quantile table gives each distribution's value at standard exceedance percentages and their return periods. Linked P% and T-years inputs give an extra value, which can be added to the table.
The results tab gathers the empirical table, the series chart, the curve image, the metrics and the quantiles, and offers a Word document download.

distinctive: Exceedance probability and return period are kept linked (T = 100/P), so either one can be typed and the other follows.
A compound mode splits the series into two parts (from a row, by a criterion column, by a value threshold or by hand), fits one distribution to each and combines them into one curve.
Fit metrics are coloured by the direction that is better for each: closeness to the empirical moments, a higher R², a lower error.
Distributions include the Krytsky–Menkel distribution and L-moment fits, as used in Russian hydrological practice.
Rounding follows the decimal precision of the source data, so quantiles are reported no more precisely than they were measured.

parts.summary: Fits one chosen distribution to each part of the series, shows each fit, and combines them into one curve weighted by the size of each part, with its own metrics and quantiles.
